certainty_reasoning: Evangelista's Y90s biography quotes their boast of being 'closer married' than the Brownings and cites it to Works and Days, p. 16 - so a participant's own testimony is underneath the sentence.
date_label: Lifelong: joint authorship from 1884 (Callirrhoe) until Cooper's death in 1913; Bradley died the following year
summary: Katharine Bradley and her niece Edith Cooper lived together, wrote together, and published everything as one poet under the single name 'Michael Field' - eight volumes of verse, some twenty-seven verse dramas, and a joint diary, Works and Days, in which they recorded their life together and boasted of being more thoroughly married than the Brownings, on the grounds that unlike the Brownings they wrote under one name. Their poems were composed separately and merged in revision until the printed voice was single. Wilde corresponded with 'Michael Field' as a single addressee between 1890 and 1893 about their verse dramas. Cooper died of cancer in 1913 and Bradley survived her by less than a year.

sources.quote: They celebrated their poetic/sexual union in several of their poems and plays, and they even boasted of being “closer married” than the more famous Victorian couple – Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning – because, unlike the Brownings, they wrote under one name (Works and Days, 16).
sources.context: Stefano Evangelista's Y90s biography, opening paragraph. 'Works and Days, 16' is Evangelista's citation to the two women's own joint diary, so the boast is theirs, not his. The preceding sentences read: 'Michael Field is the shared pen name of two women: Katharine Bradley (1846-1914) and Edith Cooper (1862-1913). Bradley and Cooper were aunt and niece but also life-long companions and lovers.'
sources.supports: Participant testimony (their diary) that the two understood their union as a marriage, and understood the single authorial name as what made it one.

sources.quote: Michael Field is the shared pen name of two women: Katharine Bradley (1846-1914) and Edith Cooper (1862-1913). Bradley and Cooper were aunt and niece but also life-long companions and lovers.
sources.context: Evangelista's opening sentences, establishing the joint pen name and the dual relation - aunt and niece, and partners.
sources.supports: The scholarly characterisation of the relationship, and the fact that 'Michael Field' is one name for two people.

sources.quote: The joint pen-name of Katherine Bradley (1846–1914) and her niece Edith Cooper (1862–1913). They published many books of poems and verse plays, none of which ever reached the stage. Among them were Callirrhoë (1884) and The Tragic Mary (1890) to which Wilde is here referring.
sources.context: Holland and Hart-Davis's identifying footnote (note 2) to Wilde's letter to 'Michael Field' of [Postmark 13 August 1890]. The editors print the forename 'Katherine'; Bradley's own and modern scholarly usage is 'Katharine'. This is the main-particulars note for both women in the Wilde apparatus.
sources.supports: Both women's dates; the aunt-niece relation; the single joint pen-name - from Wilde's own editors, i.e. independent of the Michael Field scholarship.
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 471 (printed folio 449). Transcribed from the image, en-dashes as printed.

sources.quote: Dear Michael Field, In the case of the Independent Theatre you have to rely chiefly on actors who are out of an engagement, those who have engagements being occupied or away.
sources.context: Opening of Wilde's letter to 'Michael Field', [? September 1893], on casting A Question of Memory for J. T. Grein's Independent Theatre. He signs off 'I am your sincere admirer'. Evidence of the joint identity operating socially rather than only on title pages: Wilde writes to the two of them as one man.

manuscript.repository: Princeton University Library, Princeton, New Jersey

sources.quote: Bradley and Cooper also left a vast joint diary, which they entitled Works and Days. Parts of it were published in the 1930s by their executor Thomas Sturge Moore.
sources.context: Evangelista on the diary itself. The manuscript runs to some thirty volumes (British Library, plus one at the Bodleian); Sturge Moore's 1933 selection is the published portion.
sources.supports: Locates the first-hand source: a joint diary kept by both women, of which only part is in print.

sources.quote: Sweet Wife, the hardships of early married life are beginning: let us bear them together bravely, & grow all the dearer to each other for the derision of the world. There has nothing happened to us; but what is common to all poets: let us rejoice to share their bitter herbs of adversity.
sources.context: Katharine Bradley to Edith Cooper, undated [August 1885], written the morning after a hostile Pall Mall Gazette review of their 1885 verse dramas. 'Sweet Wife' is Bradley's salutation, not an editorial gloss. The letter is Bradley's, to Cooper.
sources.supports: The 'closer married' passage in the participants' own words.
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 306 (printed folio 304) The edition names its deposits collectively rather than per letter, so this is an identification, not a transcription of a source line. Its British Library deposits are the journals (Add.ms. 46776-46804B), the Ricketts correspondence (58087, 58089) and Michael Field Correspondence vols VII-VIII (46866-46867), which the BL catalogue describes as letters with Browning and from other authors - none of them Bradley-to-Cooper. Its Bodleian deposits are the Eng. Lett. series (c.418, c.419, c.432, e.32, e.33), where the two women's letters to each other are held.
sources.speaker: Katharine Bradley

sources.quote: Of Robert and Elizabeth Barrett Browning's marriage they observed: “those two poets, man and wife, wrote alone; each wrote, but did not bless or quicken one another at their work; _we are closer married_” (Michael Field, Works and Days. From the Journal of Michael Field, ed. T. & D.C. Sturge Moore [London: John Murray, 1933], 16).
sources.context: The editors' footnote to their statement that Bradley and Cooper 'often spoke' of their relationship 'as a “marriage.”' 'we are closer married' is underlined in the original.
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 25 (printed folio 23); corroborates Works and Days p. 16.
sources.supports: Second, independent scholarly attestation of the 'closer married' passage and of its page in Works and Days.
